Ukrainian Community Day at Ashokan Center Celebrates Culture, Supports War Relief

The annual gathering raised money for children and first responders in Ukraine through the Ukrainian American Youth Association’s Hudson Valley chapter.
by Isabella Schoonover September 24, 2026September 25, 2026

In its third year, Ukrainian Community Day at The Ashokan Center wasn’t deterred by the rain.

Huddled under the shelter of the Ashokan Center’s Killian Pavilion on Sunday, about 50 community members, musicians, dancers, singers, artists and craftspeople gathered to showcase Ukrainian culture and show solidarity with those impacted by Russia’s war in Ukraine. 

The event featured performances by Ukrainian musician and songwriter Olya Friz, folk music trio Yiyi, traditional dance and music ensemble Zoloto, and others who blended traditional Eastern European folk music with modern sounds and instruments.

Half of all proceeds from the event were donated to the Hudson Valley chapter of the Ukrainian-American Youth Association. The national non-profit was founded in 1949 with a focus on providing youth education, sports, music, summer camp and cultural programs for Ukrainian-American families.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, the organization has expanded its focus to include fundraising and delivering essential supplies for children and families in Ukraine.

“This event is about community and keeping awareness that this war is continuing, because you rarely hear about it in the news anymore,” said Hudson Valley chapter leader Danylo Mykula, who is first-generation Ukrainian-American.

Danylo and his wife Katherine, a co-leader of the chapter, have spent the last five years raising funds and running supply drives to support an orphanage in Ukraine.

Through fundraising efforts like the Ukrainian Community Day, they’ve bought soaps, medicine, warm clothing, sports equipment, school backpacks and even ice cream machines for the children at the orphanage, many of whom have lost their parents in the war.

“These children have had not a lot of opportunities to be happy and enjoy stuff, so we’ve been concentrating on that,” Mykula said.

Mykula said the chapter has also sent first aid supplies, vitamins and winter coats to first responders on the front lines.

“The Ukrainian community is a tight-knit circle,” said Stephen Barankewicz, managing director of the Ukrainian Heritage Center in Kerhonkson. “That’s what we do, we stick together. We help each other out.” 

The Heritage Center prepared and served a variety of Ukrainian foods including varenyky, a Ukrainian potato dumpling, and borshch, the iconic beet and vegetable soup that’s a staple in Ukrainian cuisine.

“I’m eating borshch in the Borscht Belt. I’m so happy,” said Leo Cohen, a mandolin player in the Zoloto ensemble. The group wore sweatshirts over their embroidered Ukrainian shirts to protect them from splashes of beet-red broth.

The Catskills got its nickname from the large number of Yiddish-speaking Eastern European Jews who vacationed in the region from the turn of the 20th century to the 1970s. 

New York has the largest population of Ukrainians and Ukrainian-Americans in the U.S. at around 156,000 people, with nearly 2,000 living in Ulster County, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. New Yorkers have also taken in the most Ukrainian refugees of any other state.

Last year, Ulster County executive Jen Metzger signed an agreement to make Ulster County a “Sister Community” with the Chernivtsi Region of Ukraine. The agreement promotes mutual understanding and cultural exchange between the two regions.

Maria Sonevytsky, a professor of anthropology and music at Bard College who played the accordion with her group Zozulka at the event, said the landscape of the Catskills is reminiscent of the Carpathian Mountain range in Ukraine.

“This area, on the western side of the river and up into the Catskills, is very familiar to people from Western Ukraine,” said Sonevytsky. “That’s why, after World War II, so many people arrived in New York City as displaced persons ended up finding summer homes and establishing communities up here.”

“I think it’s amazing to have this place and there’s no other place in this country that has so many people involved in Ukrainian folk music. Like this authentic kind of folk music,” said Helyna Shepko, a first-generation Ukrainian-American and fiber artist whose daughter, Zoya, sings in the Ukrainian folk group Yiyi.

Shepko wore a hand-woven sash around her waist, which she described as a symbol of home. Her mother was born in Kharkiv, a city close to the Russian border that has suffered many attacks since Russia’s current offensive began.

Wanting to connect with her heritage, Shepko learned to weave in 2016. She traveled to Ukraine and learned from weavers who showed her traditional techniques. She now lives on a homestead where she raises sheep for wool used in her weaving, and teaches workshops around the Hudson Valley.

As she spoke, musician Olya Friz played the bandura, a Ukrainian string instrument, and taught the crowd several children’s songs in Ukrainian with the help of kids from the UAYA.

Shepko gestured to Friz.

“I think it’s beautiful to see young people interested in it, to continue,” she said. “This is what people are fighting for also, for the folk traditions.”

Photos by Roy Gumpel for The Overlook.

Isabella Schoonover is a staff reporter for The Overlook covering Woodstock, Saugerties, Hurley, and surrounding Ulster County communities. Send correspondence to isabella@theoverlooknews.com.
